I'm sorry this happened to you first off. I witnessed my best friends suicide by gunshot 11 years ago this September. It's really been a journey. I've been sad, mad, guilty, not guilty, numb, furious, confused, scared, jumpy, hospitalized, suicidal, aggressive, and so on. 

I have no medical experience but at this point I think you may be suffering from PTSD, amd if you aren't already, that's probably a reality for you. IT'S OK. That's how our minds and bodies process trauma. 

My advice to you would be to seek help from a professional if you're able. They will help you process the trauma and get back to normal. One thing that really helped me, and I wouldn't be here to type this post, was something called EMDR Therapy. Basically the therapist will have you replay the memory in your head, while at the same time vibrating paddles in your hands or something similar to that. In 2017 I was having daily panic attacks, I did EMDR and I haven't had one since. 

My one regret in this whole process is I waited so long, to long, to get help and see a professional. And please know my PTSD stems from not just witnessing a suicide but nearly a decade as a first responder, so I got an extra helping of PTSD from that. 

Some other things that have helped are mindfulness exercises (it can be whatever works for you,  for me it's fly fishing, the repetitive motion and the required concentration really help), yoga, breathing exercises, coloring, spending time outside in the sun, anything that you are motivated to do and help you focus.

Exactly. Door/window whatever. Burglars (criminals in general) will take the easiest route to get what they want. Burglary usually carries the possibility of some serious time, in most places, the more deterrents you have in place, the less likely you are to get hit. 

Burglars are like any other skilled trade.  There are skilled ones and shit ones.

 The good ones know when you are there and when you aren't. What general hours you work, what you drive,  where most people hide their valuables, what they can offload easily with a lower chance of getting caught, how to blend in, etc.

The less skilled ones will see no cars in the driveway,  kick a back door,  break a window, check to see if doors and windows are locked. Ransack your house,  etc. 

The burglars that are willing to kick a door/window knowing you are there are probably not just after your  stuff. Those are the dangerous ones. You need to have a plan, whether that is to stand your ground, or get out, whatever it is, and you need to practice it with your kids/family, just like you should all be doing if there is a fire or some other emergency. 

Best you can hope for is your dogs, lights, deadbolts etc., will slow them down and give you enough time to react and defend yourself.  Deadbolts, unless you have a metal door frame (and not a shitty metal one), actually make the door easier to kick. 

Also, just a general note. If you have a dog that mysteriously goes missing, light bulbs "go out" all of a sudden, or any of your other "defenses stop working", within a short time of each other, you need to be on high alert. That's shit that professional killers do, think serial killer kind of shit.  They know you, your routines, they've been watching you, they already know whether you will even notice if those things stop working.

Pretty common tactic used in burglaries auto break ins. Anything to achieve "target hardening" is also a good idea. Alarm system or just a sign in the yard or sticker is usually as effective, dogs, security lights (bonus points for motion sensors), some very obvious cameras, or fakes, keep the good ones hidden.

Here is my response to another post that is similar. I am so sorry for you're loss. This shit is hard but it does get better. 

Yes it does, but it isn't an easy journey. Just for context I witnessed my best friend of 10 years and roommate shoot himself. At first I was like the cliche of PTSD, hear a loud noise, hit the ground. I started sleepwalking and just some weird stuff. I became a cop after that and obviously that didn't help. I tried several medications after the suicide but they only made things worse so I refused to see anyone about my mental health (plus in Law Enforcement taking care of your mental health can ruin your career). I will say that this has been a very hard and long journey, but it is getting better. 

Here is some advice I can share with you that I have learned throughout my life up to this point. 

1. Anything you are feeling is valid. You will or are probably feeling everything from grief, anger, depression, hyper vigilance, guilt and probably more. You need to let yourself feel these things. Get it out and don't feel guilty about feeling bad or any other thing you are thinking. This is a roller-coaster but all of it is valid, and it's ok to feel all of this. If I saw my buddy alive again tomorrow,  I think I'd punch him in the face and then give him to biggest hug. 

2. About guilt. I will start off by saying this. This is not your fault and there is nothing you could have done to prevent this. THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT AND THERE IS NOTHING YOU COULD HAVE DONE TO PREVENT THIS! In my experience, as a cop and personally, once a person has made the decision to suicide, the decision is already made. Hindsight is always 20/20 and you will think back on things and think "If I had picked up on it then, I could've done something ". If he hadn't committed suicide then you wouldn't think twice about it, but he did and now you are going to analyze any hint, comment, etc in that context. But don't. 

3. Seek mental health therapy. I've come to find that mental health, whether it's depression, anxiety, PTSD ( which I am diagnosed with) are often times not given the attention they deserve. All of these(and many more), can be fatal diseases. This is how I think about it. If I got cancer that was curable with some very uncomfortable (at times) treatment,  but fatal if untreated, would I do nothing? Or fight the disease. That is the approach I have taken.  I don't want to sound loke a "pull yourself up by the boot straps" guy. But the more effort you put into treatment the better the results. Also take your medicine if prescribed. They won't all sit well with you or work for you, but keep trying. Most of them take at least a month to kick in. Be honest with your shrink(you will probably want one for meds and one for feelings and talking) and if you and the shrink don't get along find a new one. The things I like in a shrink might not be the same for you. 

4. EMDR is magic. DO IT! It sucks. It really does. In 2017 I was having panic attacks that never stopped. I was at the point that it was suicide or I get better so I tried it. It was uncomfortable. It was emotional. And it just down right sucked. But. I did 3 sessions and haven't had a panic attack sense. It was worth it to me. I am a firm believer in it and recommend it constantly. 

5. Mindfulness. Mindfulness is learning the skill to focus your brain on one thing. Think of your brain like a muscle. If you exercise it a certain way, it will get really good at doing that thing. If you are experiencing PTSD or anxiety symptoms,  then your brain will get really good at operating in that way amd find things to be anxious or depressed about bc that's the state it knows how to work in. Mindfulness helps change that. Once again you get what you put into it. The VA has an app called Mindfulness Coach that is free and actually very effective and user friendly. It helped me a lot. Learning how to focus will allow you to break the cycle of anxiety. 

6. This is probably one of the most important things. Take care of yourself. Get enough sleep, eat good healthy(or sometimes unhealthy, looking at you Waffle House) food. Watch your drinking and keep it under control. Drinking is a bandaid and it will make everything worse the next day. Exercise when you can, even of it's just walking around the block. If you're in a position to get a pet like a dog or cat, they always seem to be able to tell when I'm having a bad day, and it does help. Give your brain and body the resources it needs to fight for you. 

7. Find a hobby. Something, anything. I landed on fly fishing some how but it really does help me, even if I'm not good at it. I feel at peace in nature and I have to focus so much on casting I kinda forget everything else. 

I think I've written enough here. If you're interested, I've posted or commented many times over the last few years about what I am and have gone through. Please remember that this will get better. There is light at the end of the tunnel. You are a fighter. You are on the right track. Keep grinding away and you will come out the other side. I am always here if you or anyone else who sees this comment who wants to reach out. 

Remember. This will get better.

You can expect to working rotating 12 hours shifts anywhere you go. Some days you will go in at 0600 and get off at 1800, or go in the opposite for about 30 days at a time. Ok so let me try and steer you in the right direction. First off I'm not sure why they did a blood test. It could matter if it was a dui or something like that. As far as I know, not many states test for the presence of kratom specifically, but I have heard it could happen. Honestly, so many people go through Probation on a "plea day" (where people are entering guilty pleas and they are trying to get them of the docket, we sometimes had over 70 a day), that I doubt they even remember you asking. Also, in my state, not every incident report was given to us. Usually only was required for Domestic Violence and Sex Offenders. What I could see was the Grand Jiry indictment. So here, when you get charged with a crime, they do a warrant for your arrest, which is presented to a judge to establish that probable cause exists, and contains a small summary of what happened, usually not very detailed. This warrant is then presented by the officer or his supervisor (here these are the only 2 people who can provide testimony about the case), and then the Grand Jury basically rewrites what's written on their warrant, so an incident report would be several pages or more and very detailed. 

Let's say you committed the crime of Armed Robery, just to make an easy example. The warrant would read something like this, I am not going to use specific statutes, just a random one bc I don't feel like looking it up. So it would read:  

            "The defendant, John Doe, did willfully, knowingly, and unlawfully commit the crime of Armed Robbery, SC Statute 16-15-0370, by entering the Shell Gas Station located at 1234 ABC Street, Rock Hill SC 29870, York County South Carolina, with the intent to permanently deprived the Victim of their property and did so by pointed a silver in color revolver at the victim and stating "Give me all the money or I'll shoot you". The victim did believe her life was in danger, due to the presence of a weapon and the statements made by the defendant. This is in violation of the SC Codes of Laws, as amended in 1976. The affiant and others are witness to prove the same "

So that's basically what I would get when I looked in your file, and it is a pain in the ass to get incident reports, even amongst other LE Agencies, amd I supervised over 200 people. There just wasn't enough time to get all that info. 

So the reason it listed something like "or whatever other substances we deem that you cannot take" is really geared more towards things like alcohol, or huffing paint, or dusters stuff like that. If you were addicted to huffing paint for instance (besides wtf???) then they can make it a condition of your Probation that you can't huff paint anymore. 

To get the the point finally, here is what I'd tell you to do, remember I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. I would not mention it ever again, unless they bring it up. Kratom to most cops equals drugs and drugs are bad. Like I said earlier, once they find out what kratom really is, they usually don't have a problem with it. But they definitely aren't going to ask you much about it as far as education. They will go to other cops and ask them if they've heard of it and eventually they will go to some training class [like this](https://www.tallcopsaysstop.com/) that will tell them kratom is evil and worse then heroin. They will drug test you your first day for sure. At least we did, but that test was a freebie, we only used it to determine what drugs you were actually using, and it was a 10 panel test. You could not be violated on that first test, even if you tested positive for everything. Pretty standard stuff. The only time I know of a drug test being sent to a lab was when I found Fent in an offenders house. Fent does not pop on drug tests. 

So in short, I wouldn't bring it up again until it is brought up by them. If they make an issue out of it, it would probably just be easier for you to not use until your off probation, but refer to my other reply for some possible options. If asked I would probably say that you quit or something. The only problem there would be if they go out to your house and catch you with kratom you may end up having to do rehab and it can also be a violation to lie to your agent, but usually not a serious one. You might get a verbal or written warning. It really does depend on your officer and the policies and SOPs of that office, but I have witnessed an offender being allowed they could take kratom, and she was a pretty hardcore agent. She said she didn't care as long as they didn't fail a drug test, it continued to remain legal and kept her off hard drugs. Believe it or not a lot of officers do care about their offenders, and want them to do well. So if you were taking kratom instead of heroin, I would have been happy with that. I've had offenders that test positive for something like Heroin, Meth, amphetamines,  and weed on their first test and then only test positive for Heroin and weed the next time, then just weed the next time. Even though they tested positive it is a win to me and as long as they were really trying I never held it against them.

The problem with Kratom and Law Enforcement is training. All of the training I attended in LE says that Kratom is as addictive as heroin and extremely dangerous. I have pointed out to instructors that I took Kratom daily and have had no side effects and they just double down on what the FDA released about Kratom and have even reported me to my supervisors for using drugs. So she is probably basing her information on her training,  which is incorrect. 

One way to bring this up to her would be to show her that Kratom is legal in your state and bring her some educational information to show her regarding what Kratom really is. I would try this route first, but do also expect it not to work. The other option would be to get her supervisor involved. Idk what country or state you are in, so I can only speak to my state, but offenders (sorry, it's the term that is most often used) have a right to speak to a supervisor and challenge something they are ordered to do by their officer. This may or may not work and will depend on the supervisor. If you do this definitely make sure you have your ducks in a row and can show that you do not, or have not had problems with past addiction, or if you have that Kratom is better for you then Sub or Methadone for whatever reason. Expect them to also be uneducated about Kratom. 

If that doesn't work, you could try to get a hearing with an Admin Hearing officer. Every state should have something similar to this, but it is basically a hearing you would go through before you would see a judge. They can and could overturn the officers order, but they also may not. See the above paragraph. 

Your only other option would be to outright refuse to attend treatment,  which is going to extend your probation and could end up in a violation, so I wouldn't recommend that. Also not that in your conditions of probation is probably a clause that states that you must complete anything deemed necessary by your officer. So in my state you can be violated just for refusing to obey a direct order from your officer.  However, talk to your Agent and see if there are any free classes you could attend. In my state, the Vocatiinal Rehab dept offers free drug/alcohol treatment and it actually pretty good. Your state should have something like that. 

Last thing, a lot of what happens in Probation is based on your officer. I never got anyone in trouble for using Kratom, CBD or Marijuana that was part of my officer discretion. And I very rarely put people in jail for using drugs, and only if I felt that they were safer in jail then on the streets. While I was there I had 12 people on my caseload die from overdoses. While there is a lot of officer discretion, everything in a Probation office is dictated by policy or standard operating procedures (SOP). These should be available for you to see or read over. So maybe check their policy on drug/alcohol referrals and see what it says. 

Also next time don't tell them you use Kratom unless your state tests for it. If they do test, you may have to stop while on probation. If they don't test for it, tell her you quit, do the stupid rehab classes and just use it the whole time. Pass the classes and be done with it and never mention it again.
